# What the repowise PR bot would cost this repository, in access and in money

Established on 24 September 2026 from repowise's own documentation, its GitHub App listing, its
marketplace listing, its pricing page and the live example page it publishes. Two of the three pages
the site links, `/privacy` and `/security`, return 404, so what follows is what the public material
says and nothing more.

## What it would be granted

The GitHub App asks for **Contents: Read, Pull requests: Write, Metadata: Read, Issues: Write**. The
first of those is read access to the whole tree, not to the diff of a pull request.

## Where the code would go

The bot page says "No clone, no LLM, no token cost" and "Read-only. No code execution." The pricing
page says something different about the indexing behind it: the repository is cloned onto "an
ephemeral indexing container," parsed into a graph, and "the cloned working tree is wiped at the end of
every run," with only derived artifacts kept, documentation, dependency graphs and hotspot analysis.
Both can be true at once, the bot reading an index that an indexer cloned to build, and the material
fact is the second one: **repowise's servers would clone this private repository.**

They state they "never use your code to train any model."

## What it would cost

Public repositories are free and uncapped. **Private repositories index for free but their PR comments
require the Pro plan at 15 USD per month**, and "the bot stays silent on private-repo PRs until the
owner upgrades." So on `reijerteunis/seene`, which `gh` confirms is private, installing it buys
nothing until a subscription starts.

## The public page, which is the part nobody has ruled out

The live example, `repowise.dev/pr/repowise-dev/repowise/1204`, needs no sign-in and shows: the pull
request title and author name, the commit hash, a change-risk score and its percentile, repository
health, files changed, contracts changed with file paths and line numbers, nine outside callers in
untouched files, introduced findings by severity including complexity and error handling, primary code
authors by file with commit percentages, the test files that import the changed modules, and an
AI-versus-human authorship attribution. No source snippets, and no email addresses.

That is a public repository. Whether a private repository's page is also public **is not stated
anywhere in the public material.** The README lists "Public analysis page per PR, no sign-in" as a
feature in its comparison against CodeRabbit and Greptile, with no carve-out for private repositories,
and the bot page repeats it unqualified. The absence of a carve-out is not the same as a statement
that there is none, so this is recorded as unresolved rather than answered either way.

The ticket's first criterion asked for this to be established by looking at a private repository's
page. That cannot be done without first installing the bot on a private repository, which is the
decision being made. The honest resolution is that it is settled by asking repowise or by installing
on a throwaway private repository, and neither has been done.

## What this repository would be exposing

Not credentials: those live in Secret Manager and the pre-commit gitleaks hook exists to keep them out
of the tree. What a page of the kind above would carry, for this repository, is the shape of the trade
record schema, the names of the claims and policy-gate modules, the marketplace connector file paths,
who wrote what, and where the code is weakest. For a business whose thesis is recovering money from
marketplaces, the file names alone are a product roadmap.
